power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .01", Text = "of Replication Outcomes 211 Job Demands and Appreciation of Natural Beauty 212 Job demands were consistently a significant negative covariate of work engagement 213 (all p < .01, 𝜂2 ≈ .10-.15), whereas appreciation of natural beauty was not significant, 214 mirroring the original results."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: This study presents a conceptual replication of Popov, Popov, and Nastran (2023) (Study 2), examining whether workplace greenery is associated with work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context.
text.formatted: This study presents a conceptual replication of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov, Popov, and Nastran (2023)</ref> (Study 2), examining whether workplace greenery is associated with work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context.

text.text: Ninety-four live-in shiftworkers (55.3% women) employed in Norwegian assisted living facilities for adults with intellectual disabilities and/or autism spectrum disorders completed an online survey during autumn 2024.

Work engagement was measured with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale, and three forms of workplace greenery were assessed: window views of nature, access to outdoor natural environments, and the presence of indoor plants.
Analyses of covariance, controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty, largely replicated the original pattern of results.

Access to outdoor natural environments-both during breaks and while accompanying service users-was significantly associated with higher work engagement, whereas window views and indoor plants showed no reliable effects.
Gender did not consistently moderate these associations.
The findings provide evidence that the association between outdoor nature exposure and work engagement may extend to live-in shiftworkers and an autumn context.
Over the past decades, researchers have increasingly examined how exposure to natural environments influences employee well-being at work.

Workplace greenery, such as views of nature, access to outdoor areas, and the presence of indoor plants, has been linked to reduced stress, greater job satisfaction, and better health outcomes (e.g., Lottrup, Grahn, & Stigsdotter, 2013; Largo-Wight, Wlyudka, Merten, & Cuvelier, 2017).
text.formatted: Workplace greenery, such as views of nature, access to outdoor areas, and the presence of indoor plants, has been linked to reduced stress, greater job satisfaction, and better health outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Lottrup, Grahn, & Stigsdotter, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Largo-Wight, Wlyudka, Merten, & Cuvelier, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: From a theoretical standpoint, this can be understood in relation to Stress Reduction Theory (SRT), which posits that exposure to natural elements evokes rapid affective and physiological recovery from stress, offering a restorative counterbalance to demanding work environments (Ulrich et al., 1991), whereas Attention Restoration Theory (ART) suggests that nature's "soft fascination" replenishes depleted directed attention, thereby supporting cognitive functioning in occupational settings (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989).
text.formatted: From a theoretical standpoint, this can be understood in relation to Stress Reduction Theory (SRT), which posits that exposure to natural elements evokes rapid affective and physiological recovery from stress, offering a restorative counterbalance to demanding work environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Ulrich et al., 1991)</ref>, whereas Attention Restoration Theory (ART) suggests that nature's "soft fascination" replenishes depleted directed attention, thereby supporting cognitive functioning in occupational settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model distinguishes between job demands and job resources, suggesting that high job demands are associated with exhaustion, while a lack of job resources is associated with disengagement.
Both processes may possibly contribute to burnout.
In contrast, job resources can promote positive outcomes such as motivation and well-being (Demerouti, Bakker, Nachreiner, & Schaufeli, 2001).
text.formatted: In contrast, job resources can promote positive outcomes such as motivation and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Demerouti, Bakker, Nachreiner, & Schaufeli, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, access to nature at or near the workplace can be conceptualized as a potential job resource.

Despite promising findings, relatively few studies have focused on positive indicators of well-being such as work engagement, a motivational state characterized by vigor, dedication, and absorption (Schaufeli, Salanova, González-Romá, & Bakker, 2002).
text.formatted: Despite promising findings, relatively few studies have focused on positive indicators of well-being such as work engagement, a motivational state characterized by vigor, dedication, and absorption <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Schaufeli, Salanova, González-Romá, & Bakker, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, replication studies remain scarce in this field, raising questions about the robustness and generalizability of initial findings.
A recent contribution by Popov et al. (2023) directly addressed this gap by examining workplace greenery and employee well-being in two seasonal and occupational contexts.
text.formatted: A recent contribution by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov et al. (2023)</ref> directly addressed this gap by examining workplace greenery and employee well-being in two seasonal and occupational contexts.

text.text: In their Study 1 (Ljubljana, winter), no significant effects were found, whereas in Study 2 (Novi Sad, spring), outdoor exposure-through window views and the possibility to take breaks in natural settings-was positively associated with higher work engagement and lower burnout.
Indoor plants showed no effect in either study, and gender did not consistently moderate these associations.
These findings suggest that outdoor natural exposure may be a particularly important resource for employee well-being, but that contextual and seasonal factors could play a role.
The present study provides a conceptual replication of Study 2 from Popov et al. (2023) regarding work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context.
text.formatted: The present study provides a conceptual replication of Study 2 from <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov et al. (2023)</ref> regarding work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context.

text.text: Specifically, we examined the relationship between workplace nature exposure and work engagement among employees working live-in shifts in assisted living facilities in Norway during the autumn season.

The responsibilities of live-in shiftworkers include providing therapeutic care and supporting service users with activities of daily living, monitoring and documenting service users' needs and progress, and planning and implementing individualized interventions.
The role also involves fostering a safe, structured, and predictable living environment while managing challenging situations through preventive and de-escalation strategies.

Live-in shiftworkers (24-hour rotations across several days) represent a unique occupational group, as they spend extended periods of time at the workplace and are at elevated risk for strain and health problems associated with long shifts (Dall'Ora, Griffiths, Ball, Simon, & Aiken, 2015).
text.formatted: Live-in shiftworkers (24-hour rotations across several days) represent a unique occupational group, as they spend extended periods of time at the workplace and are at elevated risk for strain and health problems associated with long shifts <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Dall'Ora, Griffiths, Ball, Simon, & Aiken, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Replicating findings in this group is therefore important for both theoretical generalization and applied occupational health.
Consistent with the original study, we investigated three forms of workplace greenery: 1.
Window views of nature during the workday.
Access to outdoor natural environments during the workday.

As in Popov et al. (2023), we also tested whether gender moderated these associations, while controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty, two factors previously linked to well-being at work.
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov et al. (2023)</ref>, we also tested whether gender moderated these associations, while controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty, two factors previously linked to well-being at work.

text.text: Based on the original findings, we formulated the following replication hypotheses: • H1: Employees with window views of nature during breaks or while accompanying service users will report higher work engagement than employees without such views.
• H2: Employees with access to outdoor natural environments during breaks or while accompanying service users will report higher work engagement than those without.
• H3: The presence of indoor plants will not be associated with work engagement.
• H4: Gender will not significantly moderate the effects of workplace greenery on work engagement.
By conducting this replication in a different occupational and seasonal context, this study contributes to testing the robustness and boundary conditions of prior findings.
It also extends the limited literature on workplace nature exposure and work engagement, particularly in the under-studied group of live-in shiftworkers.

Because live-in shiftworkers may have more opportunities to interact with natural environments than the office workers studied by Popov et al. (2023), we expected associations in the same direction and of at least similar magnitude.
text.formatted: Because live-in shiftworkers may have more opportunities to interact with natural environments than the office workers studied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov et al. (2023)</ref>, we expected associations in the same direction and of at least similar magnitude.

text.text: Ninety-eight employees responded to the survey.
Respondents were live-in shiftworkers employed in Norwegian assisted living facilities for adults with intellectual disabilities and/or autism spectrum disorders.
Live-in shifts typically consist of 24-hour work periods over several consecutive days followed by extended time off (e.g., 3/7-4/7 rotations).
Participants were recruited between October and November 2024 via email invitations distributed through organizational managers and one company's internal
Work engagement was measured using the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES) (Schaufeli et al., 2002).

text.text: Sixteen items assessed vigor, dedication, and absorption (𝛼 = .92).
Responses were rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = never,7 = daily).
Higher scores indicate greater engagement.
Exposure to nature at work was assessed with an adapted version of the Workplace Greenery Index (Lottrup et al., 2013; Popov et al., 2023).

text.text: Three categories of exposure were examined: 1.
Window views of nature during breaks / while accompanying service users (yes/no).
Access to outdoor natural environments during breaks / while accompanying service users (no / never use / sometimes / often).
The distinction between "during breaks" and "while accompanying service users" in question 1 and 2 were included to adapt the questionnaire to the live-in shiftwork context.

text.text: Items were rated on a 5-point scale (1 = almost never,5 = almost always).
Cronbach's 𝛼 = .72.

The four-item Natural Beauty subscale from the Engagement with Beauty Scale (Diessner, Solom, Frost, Parsons, & Davidson, 2008) assessed sensitivity to and emotional engagement with natural beauty (𝛼 = .84).

text.text: Analyses of covariance were conducted in jamovi (Version 2.3.28) to test whether work engagement differed across levels of nature exposure while controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty.
Each form of exposure (view, outdoor access, indoor plants) was analyzed separately.

text.text: H1 was tested by examining the main effects of window views of nature (a) during breaks and (b) while accompanying service users.
H2 was tested by examining the main effects of access to outdoor natural environments (a) during breaks and (b) while accompanying service users.
H3 was tested by examining the main effect of indoor plants.
H4 was tested by examining the interaction effect of gender and all other independent variables listed above.
Work engagement was the dependent variable for all analyses.
Two-tailed tests were used with alpha level set to 0.05, uncorrected.

Overall, the replication was partially successful.

Consistent with Popov et al. (2023), employees who reported opportunities to spend time outdoors in natural environments-both during breaks and while accompanying service users-showed higher levels of work engagement.

text.text: No significant effects were found for window views or indoor plants, and gender did not reliably moderate any relationships.
The pattern of results is therefore consistent with the original spring study's central finding that outdoor exposure, rather than indoor greenery, was most strongly associated with work engagement.
These results provide further evidence that access to outdoor natural environments may represent an important job resource within the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model (Demerouti et al., 2001).

text.text: At the same time, several factors temper this conclusion.
The study relied on a small, self-selected sample (N = 94), which limits statistical power and the precision of effect estimates.
In particular, very few respondents lacked access to nature, reducing sensitivity for detecting view-related effects.
The cross-sectional and self-report design also precludes causal interpretation and may be influenced by response biases.
More engaged employees might be more inclined to take outdoor breaks rather than the other way around.
Although such constraints mirror those of the original study, they highlight the need for future research using experimental or longitudinal designs to establish causality.
Despite these limitations, the replication demonstrates strong conceptual correspondence with Popov et al. (2023).
text.formatted: Despite these limitations, the replication demonstrates strong conceptual correspondence with <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Popov et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Across the two studies, outdoor exposure was associated with moderate effect-size estimates (𝜂2 ≈ .06-.13), whereas findings for indoor plants and gender moderation were generally null or inconsistent.

The overall pattern is consistent with a positive association between work engagement and workplace exposure to natural environments, particularly physical access to outdoor settings, across the contexts examined.
From a methodological perspective, this replication followed the original operationalizations closely while making justified contextual adaptations for live-in shiftwork.
The inclusion of job demands and appreciation of natural beauty as covariates, as in the original design, enhances comparability.

text.text: In sum, this partial conceptual replication provides evidence that aspects of Popov et al. (2023)'s findings may extend to a different occupational group and an autumn context.

text.text: The results suggest that opportunities for outdoor exposure in residential workplaces warrant further investigation as a potential job resource.

At the same time, there remains a need for more systematic replication efforts using larger and more diverse samples, experimental design, and preferably incorporating more objective measures of exposure and engagement.

Establishing reproducible evidence about the relationships between natural environments, employee motivation, and well-being remains a key step toward a more cumulative and theory-driven environmental psychology.

For live-in shiftworkers undertaking demanding rotations, the possibility to step outside into natural surroundings could serve as a low-cost means of replenishing energy and motivation.

The weaker or absent associations for window views and indoor plants may be compatible with Attention Restoration Theory (ART) and Stress Reduction Theory (SRT), although the present study did not directly measure the restorative mechanisms proposed by these theories.
Short visual contact or passive indoor elements may not provide the "soft fascination" and "being away" experiences required for attentional recovery.
Importantly, this replication extends prior work to a new context and season.
Popov et al. (2023) collected their data in spring from a mixed-industry sample; the current data were gathered in autumn from live-in shiftworkers in health and social care.

Observing similar patterns under these distinct conditions provides evidence that the association between outdoor nature contact and work engagement may occur across different occupations and seasons.
The autumn findings indicate that the association can also be observed under conditions of more limited daylight and colder weather, although seasons were not compared experimentally.
